title.en: Dilated cardiomyopathy: the large weak pump

idea.en: Recognise a dilated thin walled ventricle with globally reduced thickening.

steps.en: What you see: The left ventricle is dilated with thin walls that thicken poorly everywhere. Ejection fraction is 40 percent or below with a low stroke volume. The mitral annulus stretches and the leaflets tether, giving functional mitral regurgitation through a structurally normal valve. In decompensation the left atrium enlarges and filling pressures rise.

Normal values with units: Left ventricular ejection fraction. Normal about 55 percent or more. Mild reduction 41 to 49 percent. Moderate reduction 30 to 40 percent. Severe reduction below 30 percent.. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification guideline, section on left ventricular ejection fraction

Left ventricular internal diameter in diastole. Normal about 42 to 58 mm in men and 38 to 52 mm in women. Above this range the cavity is dilated.. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification guideline, section on left ventricular size
Left atrial volume index. Normal 34 ml per sq m or below. Raised in decompensation with high filling pressure.. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification guideline, section on left atrial volume

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Left bundle branch block appears in advanced disease and marks dyssynchrony. Limb lead voltage is low with poor R wave progression across the chest leads. Atrial fibrillation occurs in about one in three patients.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: The first sound is soft and the apex beat is displaced outward. A third sound gallop marks decompensation. A pansystolic murmur marks the functional mitral regurgitation.

What to report: End diastolic and end systolic volumes with ejection fraction and the method used
Cavity diameters with wall thickness to show the thin dilated pattern
Mitral regurgitation grade with annulus size and tethering
Filling pressure grade, left atrial volume and right ventricular function
Red flags needing urgent referral: Pulmonary oedema or low output with severe dysfunction, needs urgent heart failure care
Sustained ventricular arrhythmia or syncope with ejection fraction below 30 percent, needs urgent rhythm review
Left ventricular clot with an embolic event, needs urgent anticoagulation review
Pitfalls: Alcohol, peripartum state, thyroid disease and tachycardia all mimic primary disease, so record causes and repeat after treatment.
Myocarditis can look identical in the acute phase, so link the echo to fever, chest pain and troponin.
A single plane ejection fraction misleads in regional disease, so always use biplane volumes.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start in the apical four chamber view and include the true apex without foreshortening.
Compare cavity size with wall thickness by eye before measuring.
Trace endocardial borders in four and two chamber views for Simpson biplane volumes.
Put colour over the mitral valve to grade the functional regurgitant jet.
Record mitral inflow and tissue Doppler to judge filling pressure.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Foreshortening the apex so volumes and ejection fraction read wrong. Fix: Slide down and laterally until the apex is the thinnest bright point and the cavity is longest. A cut apex fakes a small cavity.
Tracing trabeculation as wall so volumes read small. Fix: Lower gain until the blood pool is dark and trace the compacted border, leaving trabeculation in the cavity.
Calling ischaemic dysfunction a primary cardiomyopathy. Fix: Look for regional thinning or scar. True dilated cardiomyopathy is global, regional disease points to infarction.

q.en: A young patient shows a new dilated poorly contracting ventricle. What first?

o.en: Check for alcohol use, thyroid disease, recent pregnancy and myocarditis before labelling it primary
Start lifelong therapy on the echo alone
Repeat the echo only after five years

why.en: Secondary causes and myocarditis mimic primary disease and change management, so look for them before labelling.
